opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say moderate confidence: useful, but never something I'd trust on its own.

Sampling-based benchmarks give you a signal, but it's noisy in ways people often underestimate. When you sample with nonzero temperature, a single run can swing by a few points just from randomness, especially on small eval sets. If you compare two checkpoints and one is up by one or two percent, a lot of the time that's within the noise band. So the first thing I'd ask is: how many samples did you take, what's the variance across seeds, and is the difference actually bigger than that variance? If nobody has run multiple seeds or computed some kind of confidence interval, I treat the number as a rough hint, not a verdict.

The second issue is that benchmarks drift away from what you actually care about. Once a benchmark becomes a target, people consciously or unconsciously optimize toward it, through data mixtures or prompt formats, and the score goes up without the model really getting better. Contamination is part of that too. A checkpoint can look great on a public benchmark simply because similar data leaked into training.

So in practice I combine a few things. I use benchmarks as a coarse filter, to catch regressions or obviously broken checkpoints. Then I look at trends across many checkpoints rather than a single point, because a consistent trajectory is much more trustworthy than one spike. And then, honestly, I spend a lot of time actually using the model and reading raw outputs. You notice things that no aggregate score captures, like the model getting more verbose, more sycophantic, or weirdly brittle on certain formats.

My rule of thumb is that benchmarks are good at telling you something is wrong, and much worse at telling you something is right. You need human judgment and careful eval design on top of them.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks are not trustworthy on their own and calls a score a rough hint, not a verdict.

r002.rationale: It says a single sampling run can swing by a few points due to randomness and recommends checking variance across seeds.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, less than I used to. Sampling-based benchmarks are useful, but I treat them as a noisy signal rather than ground truth, and the noise is bigger than most people assume.

A few reasons. First, variance. If you sample at nonzero temperature and evaluate a few hundred problems, the confidence interval on your pass rate is often wider than the gap between two checkpoints you're trying to compare. People see 71.2 versus 72.5 and declare a winner, when a different random seed would have flipped the ordering. You really need many samples per problem, or many more problems, before the difference means anything.

Second, the harness matters as much as the model. Prompt format, stop tokens, how you parse the answer, whether you allow a tool call, the maximum generation length. I've seen checkpoints move several points purely because of a parsing bug or a changed chat template. So when a number moves, my first question is whether the eval changed, not whether the model changed.

Third, contamination and overfitting. Once a benchmark is popular, it ends up in training data in some form, and the score starts measuring memorization plus general capability. That doesn't make the number useless, but it stops being comparable across models trained at different times.

So what I actually do is look at a basket. Several benchmarks, multiple seeds, pass@k rather than a single pass@1, and I pay attention to the trend across checkpoints rather than any single point. If one checkpoint spikes on one eval and nothing else moves, I assume it's noise or leakage until proven otherwise. And I always pair the numbers with reading actual samples. A hundred transcripts tell you things no aggregate score will, like whether the model is getting the answer right for the wrong reasons.

The short version is that benchmarks are good for catching regressions and for ranking things that are far apart. For close calls between checkpoints, I'd rather trust a well-run head-to-head comparison with enough samples and a fixed harness than a leaderboard delta of one point.

r001.rationale: The response treats benchmark scores as a noisy signal and recommends multiple benchmarks, seeds, trends, and sample review, communicating that a score alone is insufficient to judge a checkpoint.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies variance and says a different random seed could flip the ordering between checkpoints, indicating substantial run-to-run variability.

astra-6.text: I put some confidence in them, but I wouldn’t use them alone to decide which checkpoint is better. A benchmark score depends on the prompts, the sampling settings, and how many samples you draw. So I’d want to know whether an improvement holds across repeated runs, rather than just looking at one number. And then I’d look at actual outputs: does the model make fewer mistakes on the tasks we care about? If the benchmark improves but those examples don’t, I’d be cautious about calling it progress.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it would not use benchmark scores alone to decide which checkpoint is better and would also inspect actual outputs.

r002.rationale: It says an improvement should hold across repeated runs, but does not clearly state that results have high run-to-run variance for the same model.

sol-6.1.text: I’d put some confidence in them, but I wouldn’t let a single score decide which checkpoint is better. Sampling introduces variance, so a small improvement could just be noise. I’d want to see whether the gain holds across repeated runs, how sensitive it is to the sampling settings, and whether it shows up across different kinds of tasks. Then I’d look at actual outputs: what improved, what regressed, and whether those differences matter for the intended use. A benchmark is useful evidence, but the confidence should match how robust the result is.
